subsubtopic: TRAVEL EXPENSES OF OUTGOING CHAIRMAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, who among us can honestly claim not to be fascinated by the lives of the rich and famous? Who among us is not anxious to share, however vicariously, in the excitement of high living? Now, thanks to the news of the money spent by Mr. Sirois, Chairman of Telefilm, and the many creative ways he raised funds, Canadians can dream of wildly expensive restaurants, flying first class around the world, holding gala parties, rubbing shoulders with movie stars, and spending a relaxing few days in Cannes. Oh, to be the Chairman of Telefilm!
However, what of the poor Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald)? Is it fair that she must travel in lesser style, with a modest drink from a plastic cup while up ahead in first class her Chairman flies about in absolute luxury? What are her thoughts as she hears the popping of champagne corks in first class and knows that the Chairman of Telefilm is entertaining in his usual generous way? Is she envious? Does she plan revenge? Or, will she call him to task?
Tune in again for another thrilling episode in this exciting drama of a cabinet Minister and her wayward Chairman.

subsubtopic: SUPREME COURT DECISION-CALL FOR INTRODUCTION OF NEW LAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Charter declares that Canada is founded "upon principles that recognize the supremacy of God and the rule of law". Yet, emanating from a decision by the Supreme Court, the killing of unborn children has been legalized, completely contrary to scripture.
This is not merely a question of pro-life versus pro-choice, or even the rights of unborn children versus the rights of pregnant mothers. Rather, it is whether or not anyone in Canada has the right to terminate the life of an unborn child for any reason other than fundamental justice.
Are Members of this Parliament courageous enough to base a new law on biblical teachings? If that is contrary to the Charter of Rights, then change the Charter of Rights.

subsubtopic: COST OF CLOSURE OF MONCTON MAINTENANCE SHOPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the closure of the CN rail shops in Moncton and the imminent closure of the Newfoundland Railway are but two of the most dramatic examples of the lack of commitment of Canadian National and the Government to Atlantic Canada. Twelve hundred jobs are to be lost in Moncton and 600 in Newfoundland. The Government appears content to let CN shut down operations at Moncton and yet pay over $10 million a year for up to 300 people to do nothing.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) says this makes economic sense. However, we know that CN was not even aware that it would have to pay out this money when it made the decision. This is not economic sense-it is gross mismanagement at CN and gross mismanagement by the Government of the national interest. Even government Members of Parliament from the Atlantic region have expressed their distaste and disgust at how their own Government is mishandling the issue of CN.
The Minister of Transport tells us that CN knows what it is doing with respect to closures. However, CN's actions show that it is not fully aware of its responsibility. It is time for the Government to prevent CN from downgrading service to the point that the only course of action is to auction off the Atlantic region to the private sector.
We call on the Government to force CN to spend the $250 million it will pay out to idle workers on the creation of jobs, not on their destruction.

March 30, 1988

subsubtopic: OWNERSHIP TRANSFER TO GOVERNMENT OF NORTHWEST TERRITORIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) introduced Bill C-125. This Bill transfers responsibility for and ownership of the Northern Canada Power Commission to the Government of the Northwest Territories.
Since under the Canadian constitutional system the provision and regulation of electrical energy come under provincial jurisdiction, this Bill will not only help to provide better electricity service for northerners but is also a major constitutional step forward.
Those of us who have worked for a decade and a half to achieve this transfer extend our appreciation to all those who have now made it possible.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: CLOSURE OF MONCTON MAINTENANCE SHOPS-CALL FOR RELEASE OF STUDY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to express my Party's complete disgust at the way the Government has treated the people of Moncton, especially the workers at the Canadian National Rail shops in that community. On two occasions I have seen first hand, walking down the line, the human tragedy caused by the slow death of these shops-the feeling of insecurity, the disruption to families.
Yesterday I met with representatives of the rail shop workers and gave them my complete support for a proposal to consolidate the shops in order to save the 350 jobs that still remain, and turn the remaining part of the facility into an industrial park.
I call upon the Government of Canada and the Canadian National Railway to release the internal study on which the decision to close the Moncton rail shops is purportedly based. I remind the Government that not too long ago the Deputy Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mazankowski), when he was Minister of Transport, gave his assurance that no massive layoffs would occur at these shops. He also stated that, as long as he was a Minister, the Moncton shops would never close. So much for that promise, Mr. Speaker.
I urge the Government to keep at least one promise to Atlantic Canada. Once again, I urge the Government to save those jobs at the Moncton shops.

subsubtopic: SENATE'S DELAY IN PASSING BILLS C-84 AND C-55
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last summer Parliament was recalled early to deal with a breakdown in Canada's refugee determination system. We passed Bill C-84 to supplement Bill C-55. Both Bills have had considerable discussion within this democratically elected Chamber. They would end the confusion in our refugee laws and bring some order to immigration policy.
However, neither Bill is the law of Canada and all Canadians should know why. The reason is the Canadian Senate, a group of individuals elected by no one. They have decided, against the wishes of the people of Canada, to hold up and refuse to pass Bills C-84 and C-55.
This is nothing short of a disgrace to everyone who believes in democratic principles. I hope that all of Mr. Trudeau's appointees in the Red Chamber get the message that their right to govern Canada ended in September, 1984.

subsubtopic: STATIONING OF CANADIAN FORCES IN GERMANY-OPINION OF FORMER CHIEF OF DEFENCE STAFF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, "I must say it-our forces in central Europe mean next to nothing in military terms". Those are not my words, but they might have been. Last year I took a lot of flak for suggesting that keeping a small band of Canadian troops in southwest Germany was a waste of money. In fact, I was called a neutralist, isolationist, soft-on-communism radical by a lot of Members and quite a few editorial writers in this country.
Now someone else has had the courage to challenge so-called conventional thinking. This time that someone is a man who spent his entire life defending this country. The expert who says we should be doing more to defend Canada and less in central Europe is the man appointed to command Canada's Armed Forces from 1983 to 1986, former Chief of Defence Staff, General Gerard Theriault.
Let all those who accused me last year level the same charges against General Theriault, or let them honestly reexamine their own assumptions without partisan considerations.
I want to thank General Theriault, not for agreeing with me, but for helping to raise the quality of debate on defence policy in this Chamber and in Canada.
March 30, 1988

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: CULTURAL PROPERTY-POSITION OF THE SENATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while each of the Canadian Liberal senators earns at least $67,600 a year, on average an author in this country has to make do with $10,000 a year. Still, with the outright support of their caucus the Liberal senators are denying authors, programmers, compositors and other creators the right to live decently and be protected for their creative output. Such an antidemocratic attitude on the part of the Liberal Senate must be denounced by authors, sung by singers, and publicized by programmers.
Mr. Speaker, how much longer will the Liberal Senate disregard intellectual property?

subsubtopic: PUBLICATION OF WORK DOCUMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister responsible for Canada Post released a discussion paper concerning an independent group's review of corporate rates and services. On page 15, they have this to say about the group: "Through its role and objectives the organization will have to abide by Government policies."
Mr. Speaker, Government policies as they relate to Canada Post are well known: first, deliver mail through superboxes and, second, shut down rural post offices. So what is the point of setting up such an organization if it cannot backtrack and rescind the Canada Post decision to deliver mail through superboxes and permanently lock up all rural post offices?
I endorse the suggestion that an independent group be appointed to review postal rates and services, but it must have real powers and be a lot more than a simple expedient to please the Minister.
* *
*
The Review Committee also says: "We consider that the image of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service has been tarnished by conjectures which according to our inquiries are
false."
Mr. Speaker, there will be no more unfounded allegations! Now that all Canadians are aware of the truth and that we have been to the bottom of the matter, it is obvious that doom sayers who wanted to undermine the credibility of the agency of which we can be proud will have to eat crow.
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Solicitor General for having brought the matter to light and for his leadership.

subsubtopic: AIM OF PLANNED PARENTHOOD FEDERATION OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada has launched a publicity campaign aimed at reducing the number of abortions by preventing unwanted pregnancies. In a full page ad in The Globe and Mail on the weekend, the Federation reaffirmed that the way to reduce abortions is to provide better education and clinical services, especially for teenagers who are learning about their sexuality through experience rather than through sex education programs.
Planned Parenthood has always provided excellent information on family planning and on safe contraceptive methods. It has developed an expertise in matters of sex education and reproductive health counselling. Its aim is to encourage family planning so that children will be wanted and loved, and parents will be able to provide the care that children need.
If the federal Government is really serious about reducing the number of abortions, it would support sound family planning. The Conservative Government must restore funding to the Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada to ensure that it will be able to continue its excellent work and especially sustain the most recent education campaign that it has launched.

subsubtopic: REPORT OF REVIEW COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in making public the report of the Review Committee on the activities of the Security Intelligence Service, the Solicitor General is sending a reassuring message to the labour movement. Indeed, the report indicates and I quote: It is quite clear that since July 1984, the Canadian labour movement has not been infiltrated by informers of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service.

subsubtopic: APPEAL BOARD'S DECISION TO ADMIT DESERTER FROM MEXICAN ARMY DEATH SQUAD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sickened and disgusted with the decision made by the Immigration Appeal Board in the case of Mr. Zacarias Cruz, a deserter from a Mexican Army death squad. This individual

March 30, 1988
Oral Questions
has admitted he was following orders when he personally executed 60 innocent civilians. Yet the Immigration Appeal Board chose to disregard his crimes against humanity. Has this panel any conscience, morality or sense of justice?
Canada has no room for murderers. This decision is a slap in the face to all genuine refugees and law-abiding Canadians. I remind the panel that the argument used by Mr. Cruz for committing his crimes against humanity is the same as those used by individuals who sent the Jews to their deaths. The Minister has made the right decision to eliminate the Immigration Appeal Panel because they suffer from a total lack of judgment.

subsubtopic: ONTARIO CORN PRODUCERS-DELAY IN RECEIVING CHEQUES BLAMED ON COMPUTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government instituted a Special Canadian Grains Program which it has now renewed for a second year. Unfortunately, although some farmers were paid in time, a number of corn producers in my Province of Ontario, and elsewhere, have yet to be paid. In fact some people have been waiting for $17,000 cheques since the end of January. They were told by the Department of Agriculture that they would not receive their cheques before the end of April because "the computer is not ready".
I urge the Minister of Agriculture to tell those people in his Department to get the computer ready and get those cheques out for the 28,000 corn producers in Ontario, the 6,000 corn producers in Quebec, and all the other corn producers in Canada who are waiting for their money.
They need their money. They need it now. It is the fault of the Government that agriculture is in this kind of trouble. It is up to the Government to bail them out and to do it properly.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: TURKISH NATIONALS-INQUIRY WHETHER AGREEMENT WITH QUEBEC HAS BEEN COMPLETED BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
The tragic situation of the Turks in Montreal is getting steadily worse. First they are told they can't stay in Canada, then the Minister says they can stay, and then they are told they cannot. First the Minister says he reached an agreement
with the Government of Quebec and then he turns around and says there was no such agreement.
Later, he said he had the situation under control, but this morning, we heard he did not even get in touch with the Turks in Quebec.
Has the Minister reached an agreement with the Province of Quebec, yes or no?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: TURKISH NATIONALS-INQUIRY WHETHER AGREEMENT WITH QUEBEC HAS BEEN COMPLETED BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am surprised the Leader of the Opposition doesn't have his facts straight. It isn't the first time either.
Mr. Speaker, there is no agreement between the Government of Quebec and the Government of Canada to refrain from enforcing the law. That is quite clear.
I challenge the Leader of the Opposition to find a single quote where I did not say during the last two weeks that people who are not refugees should be deported. However, the Quebec Government has the so-called Cullen-Couture Agreement signed by the Liberal Goverment in 1978, which gives Quebec the right to select immigrants abroad.
To my knowledge, the Turks he referred to are not abroad but in Montreal.
I am waiting for news from the Quebec Minister of Immigration, and Mrs. Robic is supposed to answer my letter today. I am waiting for her answer, and if the Government of Quebec does not ask to have these people-after issuing certificates abroad, we shall proceed as we must proceed in all cases of false refugee claims, that is, we will deport them.

subsubtopic: TURKISH NATIONALS-INQUIRY WHETHER AGREEMENT WITH QUEBEC HAS BEEN COMPLETED BY MINISTER
speechtext: It is obvious that we have complete anarchy in this situation, under the responsibility of the Minister.

subtopic: OPPOSITION TO BILL C-55 AND BILL C-84

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: OPPOSITION TO BILL C-55 AND BILL C-84
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister keeps blaming the Liberal Opposition and the Senate, as recited by some of his government Members under Standing Order 21, for our opposition to Bill C-55 and Bill C-84. He blames us for his problem. That is not so.
Will the Minister confirm that the position taken by the Opposition, and the position taken by the Senate, is a position endorsed by the Canadian Bar Association, most of the major church groups in Canada, the Law Reform Commission, the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, and by every expert on refugee matters in Canada, including the Minister's own special adviser on refugees, Rabbi Gunther Plaut?
Will he finally admit that Bill C-55 and Bill C-84 have nothing to do with the administrative refugee backlog that he
March 30, 1988

has allowed to build up? Will he start taking responsibility for his own inaction?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subtopic: OPPOSITION TO BILL C-55 AND BILL C-84
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the experts in this country and 80 per cent of the population want immigration laws that work. The Liberal Government has left this country in total confusion.
We have introduced legislation, and Senator Hebert himself said that the Leader of the Opposition was in favour of the Senate's obstructing bills passed by the House of Commons. Mr. Speaker, it is shocking that we should have this kind of situation in our country, and I repeat that as long as the Senators continue to obstruct legislation passed in this very House, thousands of people will be taken advantage of and come to this country claiming refugee status when they have no grounds to do so.

subtopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC-REQUEST FOR ADMINISTRATIVE REVIEW

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC-REQUEST FOR ADMINISTRATIVE REVIEW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I doubt very much whether Canadians will be totally impressed with that performance. The Minister should stop playing ping-pong with human lives. These Turkish people are human beings, and should be treated as human beings. That is the situation that I put to the Minister.
I say with the respect that 1 owe the Minister that he should not let his own pride interfere with his sense of fairness and his sense of compassion. The Province of Quebec has requested an administrative review. The Minister has turned that down. Why? What are the grounds?
The Minister also has the power under the Immigration Act to proceed on humanitarian grounds. He has turned that down. Why? Will he give us the grounds for that as well?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subtopic: PROVINCE OF QUEBEC-REQUEST FOR ADMINISTRATIVE REVIEW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I turned it down because there are thousands of Canadians who are waiting to have their relatives come to this country. They would like to follow the usual course.
Canadians do not like that people come as refugee claimants when they are not. They jump the queue in front of people who have been waiting to come here for years and years. The Hon. Member would like these people to queue jump.
[ Translation]

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
Montrealers thought last week that the nightmare of the Turkish families was over. We all believed that, in a burst of
Oral Questions
generosity, the Minister of Employment and Immigration had accepted an arrangement suggested by Mrs. Robic to avoid the deportation of the Turkish families and to accept 37 of them as immigrants.
I simply want to ask the Minister what has changed since last week and what the Minister intends to do to keep the promise made to these Turkish families.

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member said that he thought that such was the case. He should have looked closely at what I have said since last Monday. I never made any promise to anyone. I accepted the request of Mrs. Robic to suspend the deportation orders, and I did say suspend, because I must point out to the Hon. Member that the Minister has no right to cancel deportation orders. The Minister only has the power to suspend them until Quebec tells us its intentions.
At no time, and I challenge anyone to find any proof to the contrary, did I say that the deportation orders would not be respected. However, at the request of Quebec, we did agree to postpone their application.
After Quebec informs us of its decision, and the deadline is this evening, we shall proceed, as we must, to apply the deportation orders.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we can now see for ourselves that the apparent generosity of the Minister of Employment and Immigration was rather short-lasting. It lasted only long enough to buy peace in Montreal, and to ensure that the convention of the Conservative Party would take place without any problem.
What I want to ask the Minister is why he raised the hopes of the Turkish families needlessly. Why is he now giving Mrs. Robic full responsibility for finding a solution and why is he hiding behind the skirts of the Quebec Immigration Minister?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party showed so little respect for the provinces when it was in power that when another federal Government tries to apply signed agreements, these are the only types of comments the Liberals can make.
I had promised to suspend, and you should learn what the word "suspend" means, the deportation orders at the resquest of Quebec until such time as Quebec would inform us of its decision. This decision will be known today.
I repeat that, while the Hon. Member says that I am not being generous, I believe that a basic component of the law in Canadian society is the principle of justice. Everyone must be treated equally. That is exactly what we are going to do.

March 30, 1988
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-PRIME MINISTER'S SPEECH IN NEW YORK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. One year ago when President Reagan visited Canada, experts on both sides of the border agreed that, in terms of dealing with the acid rain problem, what was needed was a commitment from both countries to specific targets for reduction of levels of emission.
Instead of agreeing to that, President Reagan simply and incredibly committed himself to more research. After that, the Prime Minister of Canada, equally incredibly, described the President's policy as "very significant movement".
Since Mr. Reagan will no longer be President in November and will soon be passing from the scene, will the Prime Minister now admit that his recent speech in New York had nothing to do with trying to reduce the levels of acid rain production, but had everything to do with short run political gain for the Conservatives at home?

subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-PRIME MINISTER'S SPEECH IN NEW YORK
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it must have been a pretty good speech to draw that type of attention from my hon. friend.

subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-PRIME MINISTER'S SPEECH IN NEW YORK
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-PRIME MINISTER'S SPEECH IN NEW YORK
speechtext:
On this very important issue that we have been attempting to deal with since we were the Government, my hon. friend, the Leader of the NDP, will acknowledge that, in fact, under preceding Governments nothing had been accomplished and nothing was done here in Canada. It is a transboundary problem.
Federal and provincial Governments have agreed on a national target of reducing acid rain emissions by 50 per cent from the 1980 levels by the year 1994. This is a significant step forward.
The federal Government has signed implementing agreements with all of the concerned provinces providing for the necessary control actions. We had the results of the Special Envoy programs where, for the first time, there was-and it might not seem revolutionary to my hon. friend-a formal acknowledgement of the transboundary nature of the problem and the transboundary implications for a solution.
We have not resolved the matter in a manner that Canada deems acceptable. There is obstruction in the Congress, there is obstruction in the private sector, and, in our judgment, there is a lack of appreciation of the gravity of this in some areas of the administration.
We have put forward a treaty that we believe is in Canada's interest, and very much in the American interest, for the protection of our mutual heritage on the environmental side. We have moved this matter forward, not completely, but we
have made steady and important progress. We shall not relent until such time as we have it cleared up.
[ Translation]

subtopic: OPPORTUNITY FOR INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT ON ACID RAIN EMISSIONS
OPPORTUNITY FOR INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT ON ACID RAIN EMISSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unfortunately, the Prime Minister of Canada said the exact opposite a year ago. It was his Minister, not the Prime Minister, who criticized President Reagan last year. We are hearing some high-sounding phrases now, but no action was taken last year. That is the problem with Canada's present Prime Minister.
Since the Prime Minister is well aware that acid rain is a very serious problem for our forests, our lakes and our maple forests, why did the Government refuse to support European governments recently on an international agreement to establish acceptable emission levels for the purpose of reducing acid rain? Why the contradiction?

subtopic: OPPORTUNITY FOR INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT ON ACID RAIN EMISSIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the NDP knows perfectly well there is no contradiction here. He was here in Parliament. He saw how the Liberals did strictly nothing about acid rain for twenty years. He saw . . .

subtopic: OPPORTUNITY FOR INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT ON ACID RAIN EMISSIONS
speechtext: The Liberals did nothing!

subtopic: OPPORTUNITY FOR INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT ON ACID RAIN EMISSIONS
speechtext: No, the Liberals did nothing. He is right. He saw how the Minister of Environment (Mr. MacMillan) brought the seven eastern provinces of this country together for the first time, to agree on a major constitutional document and funding worth hundreds of millions of dollars in order to deal with the Canadian dimension of acid rain. He saw the vigorous action taken by the Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Prime Minister in dealing with the U.S. Administration. There is obstruction in the Congress and opposition from the private sector. That has yet to be resolved, but we have made substantial progress on the question of acid rain, and 1 hope we will soon be able to reach a final settlement.

subtopic: OPPORTUNITY FOR INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT ON ACID RAIN EMISSIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have said publicly in the past, and 1 repeat it now, that the Government has made significant progress within Canada as compared with the previous Government on the problems of acid rain. There is no question about that.

subtopic: OPPORTUNITY FOR INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT ON ACID RAIN EMISSIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: OPPORTUNITY FOR INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT ON ACID RAIN EMISSIONS
speechtext:
My question was pertinent to the Prime Minister's own speech when he supported the President of the United States last year, and he is making criticism this year for what he said was acceptable last year. That approach is unacceptable to us.
March 30, 1988

Mr. Speaker, my last question is for the Prime Minister. He has indicated that once again he will raise the problems of pollution in the environment with the United States during his forthcoming summit with the President of the United States.
We have a major problem with pollution in the St. Lawrence waterway and Lake Ontario, 90 per cent of which comes from the United States.
Since we already have a Clean Water Agreement with the United States, will the Prime Minister assure us that the problems of toxic waste in Lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence waterway will not only be put on the agenda but that we will be demanding some concrete action from the United States in this field?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, among the three odd questions asked by the Leader of the NDP the third is the oddest, because it does not take into account the fact that Canada and the United States just completed negotiations toward a very greatly strengthened Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement, which agreement we signed-I on behalf of the Government of Canada and Lee Thomas on behalf of the United States-in Toledo just a few months ago.
By all accounts, including the word of Great Lakes United, probably the foremost environmental group on this subject, it is a very marked improvement over past agreements negotiated by previous Governments.
In the same spirit, I am negotiating on behalf of the Government of Canada, with the full co-operation of my cabinet colleagues and the backing of the Prime Minister, with my opposite number in Quebec on an accord on the St. Lawrence because it is an integral part of the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Basin.

subsubtopic: CONVICTED TERRORIST-DELAY IN DEPORTATION HEARING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Yesterday the Minister's officials, before a hearing officer in the seeking of the deportation of Muhammad Issa Mohammad, asked for yet another delay, and this after 10 months from the time the Government made a decision to proceed.
Officials said that they had not managed to obtain a copy of the Greek pardon. Well, I obtained a copy of the Greek pardon, together with a certified translation, this morning from the Greek Embassy, and they said that government officials have not even asked for a copy yet.
Oral Questions
Would the Minister explain the unconscionable delays in dealing with this important case?
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: CONVICTED TERRORIST-DELAY IN DEPORTATION HEARING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Government and the Department of Employment and Immigration are of course determined to proceed as quickly as possible with this case. However, when the witnesses were introduced yesterday, the adjudicator demanded that other witnesses be heard instead of the witnesses that were supposed to be heard originally, so that the Department was not prepared. The only reason the case was not heard and had to be postponed again was that the witnesses present were not those who were asked to testify at the hearing yesterday.

Mr. Speaker, that is not good enough. The Government failed to turn back Mr. Mohammad in Spain. It failed to stop him at the Toronto airport. It bungled an attempt to spirit him out of Canada last month. It has demonstrated that it is not even capable of proceeding with a deportation proceeding.
How can the Canadian people have any confidence that the Government can handle the immigration responsibility?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, again, I think the problem is that the Govermment has to function in a system that is not of its own making and that is far from perfect. Furthermore, when we want to improve the system, we get systematic obstruction from the Liberal Party, which has been going on for eight months. Again, it is shocking, considering the pitiful state of the immigration system we inherited, that Opposition Members and their Leader refuse to co-operate and that there are senators who keep saying it will take months before the legislation is passed.

subtopic: QUERY WHETHER MINISTER HAS CONSULTED CANADIAN BAR AND THE SENATE
QUERY WHETHER MINISTER HAS CONSULTED CANADIAN BAR AND THE SENATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister for Employment and Immigration. The Minister himself recognizes that Canada needs effective legislation to regulate the inflow of refugees to Canada. Such is not the case with Bill C-55. On the contrary, Bill C-55 has paralysed our system and has created such delays that no other Act could be made operational.
Is the Minister willing to consult the Canadian bar and the Senate in order to amend Bill C-55 in such a way that it be made to comply with the Supreme Court decision of three years ago stating that hearings be held for each person claiming refugee status?

March 30, 1988
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subtopic: QUERY WHETHER MINISTER HAS CONSULTED CANADIAN BAR AND THE SENATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am surprised to hear the Hon. Member for Spadina refer to Bill C-55 which he has himself obstructed in the House for weeks with the help of the Liberals and which he is of course unable, imagine-even the leader of the Liberal Party cannot manage that. It is surely not in the power of a member of the NDP to convince Liberal Senators to do the work which they are supposed to be doing and which they have done for 120 years in this country, which is to abide by the will of the House of Commons.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR TO-DAY DELAY ON DEPORTATIONS
REQUEST FOR TO-DAY DELAY ON DEPORTATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am asking the Minister to consider the need for consulting to resolve a practical problem, and I am asking him if he will consider a package as follows: (1) a 60-day delay on deportation to allow time for consultation, (2) consultation with the Canadian Bar Association and the Senate to make Bill C-55 workable under our existing Constitution and Supreme Court, and (3), creation of a new administrative review that fairly identifies the people who are effectively established in Canada, taking into account help from their relatives and their work record?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR TO-DAY DELAY ON DEPORTATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have proposed and we have voted in the House on Bill C-55. The Bill has been before the Senate for six months. I will not accept any amendment as long as the Senators want to return the Bill to the House and until we see exactly what they want.
I am not sure that we need six months to make any recommendation. Once again, Bill C-55 is the one we need to deal with the backlog and particularly with those who abuse the system. Again, I do not understand why the Opposition does not support the Government in giving a Bill to the country and a system which permit us to deal with immigration.

subsubtopic: LANGUAGE TEACHERS' DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the President of the Treasury Board. The Maasai people of East Africa have the following expression: "When two bull elephants fight, it is the grass that suffers". I think that that expression applies now to the struggle of language teachers and their unions with the Treasury Board, which is causing serious problems for students and teachers in training schools across the country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-A CANADIAN HYDROGEN AUTHORITY
speechtext:
That the Government consider the advisability of introducing legislation to establish a Canadian Hydrogen Authority which would report directly to the Minister of State for Science and Technology and whose mandate would empower it to:
(a)	initiate, coordinate and oversee the research and development implied by a commitment from the government to undertake a Hydrogen Mission;
(b)	consult with representatives of industry, government, labour, academia and other relevant groups in order to set an agenda determining the priorities and goals of the Mission with respect to research and the establishment of Canadian leadership in the development and production of hydrogen technology; and
(c)	create a timetable according to which major projects crucial to the Mission's success are to be undertaken and completed.
He said: Madam Speaker, I hope that the scheduling of an attractive diversion by the Speaker is not a sign of the regard in which this motion is held. Nevertheless, it is with enthusiasm I rise today to address the motion concerning the creation of a Canadian Hydrogen Authority. Ultimately, of course, the decision to establish such an authority would be part of a much bigger commitment by the Canadian Government to undertake a National Hydrogen Mission.

In recent years we have heard a lot about industrial strategies. A national mission would define a strategy and provide an approach, a vision, a philosophy. The report on Hydrogen a national mission for Canada, is an excellent illustration of this kind of mission, an example of the way we ought to come to grips with the over-all problem of economic development.
First I should like to comment briefly on this idea of a national mission before dealing more specifically with the role of hydrogen in this strategy.
Madam Speaker, we have all heard the rather strange cliche that Canadians are supposed to be levers of wood and drawers of water. There is a certain fatalist truth to that, but it is true as well that we belong to the international fraternity when it comes to some of the newest technologies such as telecommunications, aerospace, computer science, and electronics. Clearly we are making progress and we do have what it takes to be a lot more than what the cliche would make us appear to be.

March 30, 1988
Supply
Nonetheless it is a fact that a sizeable number of our economic sectors are directly related to the extraction and export of natural resources, to the extent that we are prisoners of the vagaries of international demand and the sharp fluctuations of the price of raw materials.
This has been painfully obvious over the past five years. On the one hand, the economy of Ontario and that of Quebec-to a degree-with their leading manufacturing sectors, have been expanding at an accelerated pace despite the world recession.
On the other hand, the Atlantic provinces, the Prairies and the West Coast, dependent as they are on raw material exports, have been at a disadvantage due to the price of raw materials in international markets.
All this to say, of course, that those economies must become less dependent on raw material exports. But the question remains: Plow?

The advice one usually gets at this point is that diversification must build on existing strengths, which translates into the view that a manufacturing sector should be developed which is based upon reasonably strong resource industries. Thus far the advice is sound. However, a key question needs answering.
When we speak of the creation of a manufacturing sector, what kind of beast do we have in mind? Is it the kind of manufacturing which creates jobs based on secondary manufacturing through the processing of fish, wood or other resources? Perhaps, in part. But these will not replace the many jobs lost to such things as cheaper labour costs in Southeast Asian countries like South Korea, Taiwan and Singapore, with which we must compete.
Is it then capital intensive as is the case of computerized automobile assembly plants or oil refineries? If so, it probably requires that governments attract investors, mainly foreign, by providing generous tax concessions to offset the costs of locating large projects in this or that region of the country.
This strategy, rather than solving problems, really plays into the hands of our competitors. For if the over-all goal of diversification is greater local control of the economy and protection against the whims of the market, the strategy fails. It simply shifts the dependence from one external player to another. It is the owners, not the community, who control the factory's future and to that extent the local economy.
Moreover, far from injecting capital into the national economy by removing profits from the country, it may well drain it. The good thing about such projects is that once construction is finished, away they go. The whole package- products, markets and jobs-is there and functioning in the shortest possible time. For a politician who looks no farther than the next election, this is of course an attractive feature.
In large measure this is the Government's strategy. It is the promise and the danger in the free trade pact. In fact, importing packages holus-bolus creates rather than solves problems in the national economy. It may be a temporary shot in the arm for such and such a town, but in the long run permanent solutions cannot be based on quick fixes. They must evolve from the ground up, developing the strengths and special advantages of the local economy. They must merge into the broader regional and national economies to form a single, cohesive and integrated system which is given direction in some way.
Therefore, if we are serious about diversification, we must ask what is on the horizon. If we want to develop, it must be toward the future, not toward the past. It does not take much looking to see that the economies of the future will be dominated by highly sophisticated, knowledge intensive industries. Developed countries are weaning themselves of their dependence on natural resources and the manufacture of labour intensive products and replacing them with products and services which are knowledge intensive. In order to remain a developed country then, Canadians will have to make this transition.
This is a real challenge. As the recent report of the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology has stated, we do not presently lead in any area of international science or technology. In spite of the engineering feats involved in the creation of, say the Canadarm, our expertise tends to be limited to the mastery of a narrow range of scientific and technological areas. In short, however good a job we are doing at working at someone else's claim, Canadians are not staking out their own territory in the scientific and technological frontiers.
Indeed, it has become a dominant strategy for Canadians to look for niches in existing markets which they can fill. In making the transition to a knowledge based economy then, we can if we wish continue the tried and true strategy of finding small holes in someone else's initiatives which we can specialize in filling. It is a proven strategy. Of course, the disadvantage is that it places us permanently in the shadow of bigger players.
The alternative is for us to strike out on our own and choose an area which can capitalize on our existing strengths instead of targeting small niches in already crowded markets. By adopting a broad strategy to develop and manage an emerging industry we can stake out our own fertile territory and cultivate it for the markets it will eventually produce. If a new area of economic development really is emerging, opportunities will abound. We need only to recognize them and have the initiative to exploit them.
March 30, 1988

In this respect our place in history would not be unlike our early settlers and entrepreneurs who created from the wilderness a nation united by railways and roads and whose economic prosperity was powered by vast resources of timber, coal, fish, minerals and so on.
Let us be candid. The creation of a new, knowledge intensive, sunrise industry is a major undertaking. It requires massive investment in research and development to build the technologies and expertise on which the new industry is based. But research and development take time. As a result there is usually a significant time gap between investment and dividend. Private investors, however, like to see quick returns on their money. They are, at best, reluctant to make long-term investments in research and development even when the sum is, relatively speaking, small.
When we start talking about billion dollar outlays to found a new industry, we simply cannot count on them to pick up the ball and run. In spite of what some economists may say, we have learned through bitter experience that one thing market forces cannot be relied upon to guarantee is innovation depending upon large-scale scientific research and development. We certainly cannot move from the premise that an opportunity, even a golden opportunity, exists in a market system to the conclusion that therefore it will be exploited. Perhaps an example will make this point.
Consider Japan's commitment to develop a fifth generation computer. This is a multibillion dollar investment which over the 10 or so years it will take to develop will unquestionably repay few dividends. It is extremely doubtful therefore that any single company or consortium of companies would have undertaken the project on its own. But in order to consolidate the country's position as a world leader in the industry the Japanese Government mobilized members of business, academia and Government and united them around the common goal of making Japan the first country to develop a fifth generation computer. This type of collective effort by members from all sectors of the community and led by Government can be called a national mission.
Canada, too, needs a national mission. Some think that our participation in the U.S. space station is such a mission for Canada. It is not. The reason why it is not is clear. A national mission is distinctly the possession of that nation which undertakes it. When the mission is extended beyond the nation it ceases to appeal to the inner sense of pride, duty and, most important, of self which sustains it.
The space station is an American initiative. Even though Canadians participate in it, we neither control nor direct it. Although Canadians can take pride in their contribution to the American space program, it is still the other guy's show.
Hence a national mission is a broadly based, government led strategy which aims at mobilizing diverse sectors of society and uniting them around a common goal. This sense of participating in a collective undertaking is crucial. This is what binds a project together and gives it a special momentum, a
Supply
sense of potential national accomplishment. As such, it is the highest form of nation building.
I think I have said enough for the moment about the concept of a national mission to give other Hon. Members a pretty good idea of what I am talking about. I therefore want to move on to propose what that national mission for Canada might be. Before doing so it might be helpful to recap what I have said.
There is a transformation now under way in developed nations in the direction of knowledge based economies. Knowledge intensive industries result from innovative application of new scientific and technological knowledge. Staking out and developing one of these areas would allow Canadians to create and to establish a new industry. This is however a large scale long term costly venture requiring substantial investment in research and development. Because of this, private investors are unlikely to undertake such a project alone. Yet there is a golden opportunity for Canadians to move out of the shadows of their industrial big brothers and become a major player in the new economic order.
To do so we need the co-operation and participation of business, academia, Government, labour and so on. This can only be achieved through strong leadership provided by the federal Government under the auspices of a national mission.
I now turn to the question of hydrogen as that national mission. If Canadians want to undertake a national mission to develop a new national industry, quite simply stated that new industry should reside in the development of hydrogen technology, since hydrogen will be the energy currency of the future.
As we are all aware, the world's main energy source is fossil fuels, or as some of my friends prefer to call it, old dead dinosaurs. We also know that there are only so many dinosaurs-

speechtext:
It has been suggested that certain Liberals believe that some of the dinosaurs have survived in the backbenches of the Conservative Party.
One thing we know, it will not be very long before we have to go to museums to find dinosaurs. In short, we are running out of fossil fuels.
But there is an even more urgent and frightening concern about fossil fuels, and that is pollution. First, the burning of fossil fuels gives us the smoggy, noxious environments of large urban centres; second, they produce acid rain. We have discovered that we are not only killing ourselves by breathing sulphur dioxide, we are also killing our lakes, rivers, forests, and everything in them.
As though this were not bad enough, we are visited by another, third, plague, the greenhouse effect, the carbon dioxide build-up in the atmosphere. If it continues at the

March 30, 1988
Supply
present rate, it will drastically alter the climatic conditions and cycles of the entire planet by the middle of the next century, if not before. It means massive flooding or droughts and drastic changes to crop conditions around the world. The result would be economic chaos.
The conclusion is that depleting stocks and environmental destruction will force us to seek alternative fuels. This is where hydrogen comes in. To see why hydrogen is so important, a distinction must be made between sources of energy and energy currencies. The former includes things like coal, crude oil, hydroelectric power, uranium, sunlight and wind. The latter refers to the forms which energy takes. Thus, electrical energy being derived from sources such as wind or coal is an energy currency, not a source. Future energy needs will have to be satisfied by currencies which are non-pollutants and derived from renewable sources.
Hydrogen is an energy currency, not a source. Like electricity, it can be derived from a vast variety of renewable resources such as hydro, wind and solar. Moreover, while electricity stills looms large in the energy picture, hydrogen will inevitably play an increasingly important and complementary role.
There are three reasons for this. First, there are major tasks, such as serving as a chemical or material feedstock, which electricity cannot perform. Second, while hydrogen can be stored and transported in large quantities, electricity cannot. Lastly, there is no other known chemical currency which can be manufactured in large quantities from renewable resources.
This last point is especially important. It means that hydrogen is the inevitable choice as a feedstock in the future production of chemical commodities. This virtually guarantees the need for highly sophisticated technology to serve a multibillion dollar market. If Canadians are the first to develop that technology, they will have virtually unfettered domination of that market. Indeed, in Canada alone, hydrogen is already a one billion dollar a year industry, fully one half of which is accounted for in the manufacture of chemical products. This means that the technology is already under development.
I spoke earlier about the delay between investment and return when developing new industries. In fact, one of the great virtues of developing and marketing hydrogen technology is that the transition to the hydrogen age will be made in stages. This means that we can expect significant early returns on some investments and, equally important, permits us to develop our markets a stage at a time as these new technologies and products are phased-in.
Hydrogen technology is already widely employed in the production of just those fossil fuels which will eventually be replaced. In Alberta, it is now used in the upgrading of heavy oil from the tar sands; 30 per cent of our domestic use of hydrogen is in the petroleum and petrochemical industries. In other words, a commitment to develop hydrogen technology is not like stepping out into virgin territory. We can actually work toward the development of the new industry in and
through the old one. This is consistent with the idea of building on existing strengths.
We are now on the verge of signing a deal which would purchase, at a cost of $8 to $12 billion, imported technology to build nuclear powered submarines. Would it not make more sense to invest that money in the development of a hydrogen fuel cell? A submarine powered by such a fuel cell would have under-ice capability at least equal to that of a nuclear powered submarine. It would have the added advantage of not giving off any heat exhaust by which it might be detected by the enemy. This could be an opportunity for Canadians to develop a home-grown technology which would render the current nuclear technology obsolete. Moreover, such a fuel cell could also be used to power automobiles, locomotives, aircrafts, rockets, and other types of marine vessels.
The potential applications of a hydrogen fuel cell to vehicles is nothing short of spectacular. Canada, which already has an established automobile manufacturing industry, could develop a prototype, a non-polluting vehicle. The marketing of a hydrogen powered vehicle would be a ground breaking effort in the battle against pollution, and consumers could not be held hostage to the threat of diminishing fuel supplies and rising fuel costs.
As for our natural advantages, Canada's vast hydro resources in provinces like Quebec, Manitoba, British Columbia, and Ontario provide ideal locations in which to situate a plant to manufacture hydrogen by electrolytic conversion from renewable sources. It is worth noting here that Quebec has had a long standing interest in the potential of hydrogen as providing a market for its hydroelectric resources.
[Translation\
Premier Bourassa in fact mentioned in his book entitled L'energie, du Nord (Power from the North) the possibility of developing the hydrogen market. Just recently, the Government announced a $7.5 billion investment to develop James Bay and launched a study into the possibility of developing appropriate technology to transport large quantities of hydrogen by sea.

We have outlined the possibility for an industrial strategy for Canada based upon hydrogen technology. It is still early in the game. We are asking of this country to accept the challenge that will make us not a sharer in the missions of other nations, but to establish a mission of our own based on strengths that we already have.
The existing petrochemical industry already is based in large measure on the use of hydrogen generated from methane. Some day it can be produced through the hydroelectric power that so characterizes many parts of our country. It is a fuel of the future, one that is renewable in its source, and nonpolluting. At a time when we need new energy sources and new energy currencies, at a time when we need to attack the problem of pollution, we have made a proposal here now
March 30, 1988

before you, Madam Speaker, that can put Canada, for the first time in its history, in first place, to the benefit of the entire country and every citizen in it.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the kind comments of the Hon. Member. He has asked a great number of questions and has made a number of remarks to which I would be pleased to attempt to respond.
1 am certainly cognizant of the fact that the study was commissioned by the Government. I am also cognizant of the fact that the former Minister of State for Science and Technology cancelled the $10 million alternative energy program within the NRC. This was an act which was not consistent with the ideas even then existing about the potential of hydrogen technology as an area that could constitute the Canadian mission.
In referring to the notion of a mission, I should like to reemphasize the importance of it being a Canadian mission. As the Hon. Member knows, the author of the report indicated that it was fundamental to the mission that Canada own the technology that was developed. Obviously that has certain significances in respect of the free trade agreement and the conditions of ownership and control with regard to technology. We would hope that the industry would be in a position to sell technology to the rest of the world.
The Hon. Member asked which specific application of hydrogen technology I would most support. Of course he knows that as matters now are we have developed considerably in the area of hydrogen technology in connection with the hydrogenation of heavy petroleum from methane.
The chief source of hydrogen in the country is methane, which is a relatively expensive source in terms of the kinds of usages that might be projected. Ultimately, as fossil fuels run out, hydroelectrically produced hydrogen would be in a position in terms of cost and general economies of scale to replace those fuels for a number of ordinary fuel uses.
However, apart from developing the technology of hydrogen transport, storage, and so on, in alluding to the potential for hydrogen driven marine vessels-and specifically submarines were cited-it is an area that should be explored as soon as possible. Heavy locomotive vehicles, whether they be trains, submarines, rockets, or airplanes, are areas of the future in which we could establish our place in respect of alternative applications of hydrogen in new forms of motive power through the application of the fuel cell and other applications with which I am sure the Hon. Member is familiar.
If I were looking to the future and immediate prospects for big jumps in our advantage, those are the areas where I would seek Canadian advantage.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the initial kind words of my hon. colleague, a scientist and parliamentarian whom I respect very much. I am surprised that he chose to divert the discussion to quite crafty political considerations which were entirely wrong.
I did not say that the fuel cell should be the only priority. Nor did I suggest that submarines should be the priority for the application of fuel cells. Let me tell the Hon. Member that it is a fact of New Democratic defence policy, which we suggested, that we indeed buy conventional, not nuclear, submarines.
It seems to me that the Government's notion of buying nuclear submarines could have this best appraisal placed upon it

that it seeks submarines with the capacity of staying submerged for long periods of time, and hydrogen powered submarines would have that quality. The Hon. Member is wrong on two counts.
In respect of funding, if the Government restored the $10 million that it has already cut from alternative energy research, it would be a good start in getting the authority started on its job.
Hon. Frank Oberle (Minister of State (Science and
Technology)): Madam Speaker, I am rather pleased to join in the debate this afternoon. I am thankful that the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) placed this interesting, challenging, and important topic on the agenda of the House of Commons. I am also thankful for his putting it in such a responsible, conciliatory, and non-combative fashion. Perhaps at the end of my speech I will tell him that I have no problem agreeing with almost all the principles in his motion, and I know that should please him. I know that it would please Dr. Scott, the author of this important report who is in the gallery, a former colleague, Gordon Gilchrist, and others who spent a lot of time contemplating the exciting prospect of making Canada a world leader in hydrogen technology and of having in place a national mission for the development of hydrogen in its many dimensions.
Having said that, I would be remiss if I did not engage in setting the stage and showing a larger picture of the country's national policy and national strategy within which such a hydrogen mission could be placed.
I just returned from a week-long trip, and as it happened, it coincided with a number of meetings that I had. First, I met with the Council of Science and Technology Ministers of the provinces and territories in Edmonton last Friday. Then I travelled to Vancouver on Monday. We had one of the first of five regional follow-up conferences to the national conference in Toronto in which the Hon. Member participated in part. That conference created such enthusiasm and excitement through the country. Then on Tuesday, I chaired, on behalf of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), a meeting of his personal advisory council, the National Advisory Council on Science and Technology. Then I had to fly back overnight to be here because I wanted to participate in this debate. I say this as a compliment to the Hon. Member, because it is very timely to discuss this.
As the Hon. Member knows, we are discussing the priorities of the Government. We have spent a lot of time and effort at the Standing Committee, and the Hon. Member participated in some of that. For the first time, the committee spoke of issues like this, giving Canadians an opportunity to bring the message to Government through the standing committee, in fact, the standing committee looked at the hydrogen report and gave it excellent marks.
I have said these things because the National Advisory Council the Prime Minister appointed dealt with the subject as well, as have all the other like bodies. It is not anything new. In fact, as the Hon. Member knows, there have been previous such studies. One of them was done within the context of the
March 30, 1988

alternative energy task force on substitutes dating back to the 70s when we were suffering from the energy crisis and were looking for future energy sources. All of these things have come together and we have created quite a bit of interest throughout the country.
As I said, we have also spent a lot of time doing precisely what the Elon. Member has suggested is urgent for the country, and that is to develop a national thrust, a focus, a policy and a strategy that will take us from where we are into the new information age. The Hon. Member has said that hydrogen will be the energy currency, and I say that information and knowledge will be the currency that drives the new age. He has no disagreement with that.
I just happen to disagree with the Hon. Member on one point. He said in his speech that he does not believe that the private sector could, on its own, provide the necessary impetus to do the type of innovation that would be necessary. 1 say to him that only the private sector can do that. If the public sector could do it, we would not have any worries. We have attempted to do it for so many years but it has not worked.
Unless there is co-operation between the universities, the private sector and government labs, and unless we have the resources and the correct climate created through the leadership of the federal Government, I recognize that readily, nothing will happen. We will not get that required cooperation if we continue to tell the private sector to wait for us to do it, and then we will call on it whenever we are ready to pass on some of the benefits. The private sector will have to take the lead, and we intend in fact to involve the private sector very much in every stage of our future plans and programs.
The Hon. Member recognized this readily. I liked his speech because it reflected a number of the phrases I have used myself, and the Prime Minister has used in speeches, including the phrases "national trust", "national strategy", "moving into the information age" and "finding ways to diversify our economy". These phrases are indeed in line with the advice we have been receiving, the advice we have tested against the group of eminent Canadians who came together in Toronto for three days to work with the Prime Minister.
We confirmed a consensus. We looked at the principles we had identified as being the basis of a national thrust. We unveiled the policy as we see it unfolding for the role Canada will play in this new knowledge and information age. We have a national consensus and it is being celebrated throughout the country. We are rather pleased about that, because without that kind of a mobilization of all the geniuses in Canada, and without the commitment of all the stakeholders including the private sector, the provinces, universities and the federal Government, we will not be able to respond to the challenges and opportunities that exist.
What are some of our priorities? The forces we are attempting to manage and control are changing in such a revolutionary fashion. There are new market forces in the world. It
Supply
became quite clear to us, as it always has been, that any policy would have to be consistent with what one might consider to be distinctively Canadian cultural values and attitudes. Any policy would have to be consistent with what Canadians consider their role to be.
Each nation has different priorities and different attitudes. The United States, for instance, sees itself as the custodian of liberty and freedom throughout the world. That is why the national Government in the United States spends 75 per cent of its research money on defence. Thank God the Americans do that, because they have helped the rest of the free world to bring about stability and peace for a period unprecedented in history.
Canadians have priorities that are somewhat different. We love our environment. We take our custodial practices over the wealth of our natural resources very seriously. Those are the priorities of Canadians.
We set out to show leadership in developing a national policy and a national strategy consistent with Canadian values. We have introduced a number of principles that underlie the national strategy. My hon. friend from Windsor-Walkerville knows of these principles. They are those included in the national policy which was signed by 10 provinces and the territories with the federal Government, the innovative action strategy.
In that strategy, one of the principles is industrial innovation and technological diffusion. The other is the effective management of federal resources, a principle that is not insignificant. This year, $4.5 billion was spent on research for development in science-related activities intramurally. The third principle is the development of the necessary highly qualified people. This requires university training. The fourth principle is public education and public awareness of the concept of a science culture, something which is critically important. Finally, of course, there is the principle of the development of our strategic technologies.
The Hon. Member has mentioned hydrogen as being a possible strategic technology. Frankly, I am as enthusiastic as he is about that particular prospect. We have done all kinds of things. We have not just consulted and planned. Canada could not wait, nor were we prepared to wait, until all the studies were complete and every Canadian had been consulted to ensure that what we are doing will be consistent with these attitudes and will in the end mobilize and inspire Canadians to join in this national mission. We did take some actions, particularly in the strategic technologies. There is the microelectronics technology to which we committed $90 million. There is the biotechnology thrust that is now gaining much momentum. There is the work that is going on in advanced materials.
How does that all tie in with what we are discussing here today? First, in light of what I said, we want to look at the proposals in Dr. Scott's report, in the report of the standing committee and in the report of the alternate fuel committee.

March 30, 1988

How would that tie in to this kind of national thrust? First, I said Canadians love the environment. We take our custodial responsibility very seriously. We have always paid a lot of attention to energy security. We live in a northern climate and every home which provides the kind of comfort and security you want has to have, in our country at least, a proper heating system. Energy has always been critically important and it has always been in the back of Canadians' minds. That is why we developed, for example, the tar sands technology far in advance of everyone else.
The Hon. Member says we have never done anything. With respect, we have the best nuclear technology in the world. The CANDU reactor is still the most efficient and safest nuclear generating system in the world. There is no doubt about that in anyone's mind.
We are the third nation in space. Why? Because of a Canadian national mission involving fascination with the idea of bridging distances and bringing our people together from coast to coast. That is why we are world leaders in transportation and communications technology. That is why we were the first nation in the world to have our own communications satellite in space.
Canadians have had all kinds of national missions in the past and I do not accept for one minute that we have never done anything or will never in the future be able to do anything. Quite the contrary. As I travel the world and meet with my counterparts in Europe and Asia I am a big wheel. It is just that Canadians at home do not understand that and have yet to celebrate the fact that we are quite good at what we do when we set our minds to turning adversity into opportunity.
Why hydrogen? Because we think seriously about energy security, we would like to find a replacement for conventional fuels which are polluting the environment. It is not just our own environment, it is the world environment. We hear alarmist reports all the time about what might happen to the ozone layer if we insist on using conventional fuels. We would like to replace the harmful chemicals we use in agriculture and forestry with perhaps biofertilizers, pesticides and herbicides. Hydrogen can play an important role in lessening our dependence upon traditional fuels.
Of course, we are uniquely positioned to take a lead in the world in the production, storage and development uses of hydrogen, but it is hardly a new idea. I am told that the Germans are launching this year a hydrogen submarine. It is not hydrogen propelled but it is used to control the environment inside the submarine. Several car manufacturers in Europe are testing hydrogen engines.
With respect to propulsion technology, we have perhaps missed a connection, but there is an exciting aspect to all this in developing strategic partnerships and alliances with other industrial countries in using our technology. We are the
biggest user of hydrogen. There is a $1 billion market right here. We are using it for the upgrading of the tar sands and heavy oil production. It is of course the fuel that space rockets and other vehicles will be propelled by. That is nothing new. It is happening now.
We could develop some strategic alliances and partnerships to carve out that part of the hydrogen mission unique to us. First, we have lots of natural gas. We have an abundance of hydroelectricity which other countries do not have. We could literally take electricity, turn it into hydrogen, and export it to regenerate electricity. You could export electricity not just to California or New York but all over the world.
Everyone likes to be a little bit of a futurist and I can see us 30 or 50 years from now driving down to the grocery store to pick up a fuel cell and plug it into the side of our car. It is all right there and Canada could play an important role.
What is the hold-up? Let me tell the Hon. Member there is no hold-up. Let me tell my colleague that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) and I have invited to Ottawa within the next few weeks a number of people representing various sectors of the economy, including some academics, who could help us design the next step. We have consulted and will continue to consult with industry. We have a national hydrogen council which has been working for many years, and public utilities, energy companies and so on, who have given us valuable advice.
I want to thank the Hon. Member for putting his motion on the table. As he knows, a former colleague of ours, Mr. Gilchrist, worked closely with Dr. Scott. He is one of the authors of the report. My hon. friend from Bruce-Grey is one of the early instigators of mobilizing the keenest people in the country to help us put this report together. There is no holdup.
However, hydrogen is not the only thing we need to keep us on the crest of the wave sweeping mankind towards the next century in this new age. There are other priorities.
As the Hon. Member knows, we have not been reluctant to make tough decisions. We have stabilized university funding. With private sector support we have increased it over five years by over $1 billion. Just a month ago in Toronto the Prime Minister announced $1.3 billion in additional funding for science and technology over the next five years. I have already told the Hon. Member about the micro-electronic strategy costing $90 million. We put $28 million into the industrial assistance program last year. Some $30 million went to the unsolicited proposals program. In all, in the current fiscal year, we will be increasing spending in real terms by over 5 per cent or $2.6 billion. That is not an insignificant response to the challenges the Hon. Member has identified and with which I agree.
I thank him for his support because this issue will be raised again. Of course, one of the principles of the national strategy is public awareness and culture building. People are listening
March 30, 1988

to this debate today and that will tend to help. It must be encouraging to Canadians to know that when we talk about the future of our country and a truly national mission, we can put partisanship aside and talk about a national thrust in a cohesive fashion. I think this could be one such thrust. As soon as our dialogue with the decision-makers who have to make it happen is complete, I hope to have some very good news for the Hon. Member and all Canadians. I hope that hydrogen can truly become one of our great national missions.
