speechtext:
Madam Speaker, before I begin with the remarks I had prepared, I want to comment on something the Minister said during his speech. He said that the Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) said that the private sector cannot do it. The Minister replied that only the private sector can do it. He then referred to the necessity for leadership on the part of the Government.
There is not only a need for leadership on the part of the Government, there is a need for funding for this kind of research that will develop the use of hydrogen in Canada.
It is common knowledge that in basic research in many countries in the world Governments are funding major research programs in long-term applied research. I recall an interview that Fraser Mustard, President of the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research, gave at the time that Canada announced its participation in the space station. He said that it was a myth to think that this research in the United States was funded by the private sector. All of the funding for this longterm applied research and high risk research, which will only pay dividends 10 or 15 years down the road, comes from Government.
I want to remind the Minister that this kind of program will not be launched without adequate financial resources committed by the Government to spur private sector initiative.
I want to thank the Member for Windsor-Walkerville for having introduced this subject for debate today. Let me say that I agree with him that there are sound economic and environmental reasons for pursuing the development of hydrogen as an energy source.
First let us deal with the environmental considerations. We all know that the most expensive way to deal with pollution is to clean up the environment once it has been polluted. It may be impossible to do so in some cases, such as with carbon dioxide that is released into the atmosphere. It is also expensive to remove pollutants at the time they are produced. An example of this is the installation of scrubbers or other technology in some of our coal-burning plants.
It is least expensive and obviously most sound from the point of view of the environment to use a process which does not produce pollution. We avoid the problem by burning clean fuel. The significance of hydrogen is that it is the only fuel which produces nothing but water vapour when burning. There are sound environmental reasons for pursuing the development of hydrogen as an energy source.
There are also economic considerations. As I understand the report of the Advisory Group on Hydrogen Opportunities, in suggesting a national mission in the area of hydrogen for Canada they are saying that we would not only be protecting the environment, we will be building our energy future by embarking on such a national mission. In spite of the current oil glut, fossil fuels will run out at some point in our future. There are varying estimates on when that may occur, but certainly there could be shortages caused by man-made disasters or wars in the very near future. We could experience the kind of shortages that were caused as a result of the Arab oil embargo in 1973, and again in 1979.
Apart from the shortages caused by wars or embargos, there is the reality that fossil fuels will run out. The country which will be ready to operate without them or extend the supply of fossil fuels will have a tremendous competitive energy advantage.
The other advantage that was pointed out by the Advisory Group on Hydrogen Opportunities is that hydrogen as a future energy fuel will need a technology. There will need to be a whole technological infrastructure to make its use practical. Quite clearly, the first country to develop that technology will be able to sell it to the world.
These are what I understand to be some of the considerations that are being put forward by the Advisory Group on Hydrogen Opportunities. While I agree with the Member for Windsor-Walkerville that we should seriously consider adopting the development of hydrogen as a national mission, there are obviously difficulties and sacrifices that will have to be made in the adoption of any such national mission. These
March 30, 1988

difficulties in respect to Canada are compounded by some of the very shortsighted budget cuts that were made by the Conservative Government after taking office in 1984.
There was an energy division at the National Research Council which was engaged in research primarily in the area of renewable energy. This division was totally disbanded.
Figures which I believe relate to hydrogen indicate that in 1984 a program was founded at some $9.6 million. The work was mainly being done at the NRC, but some research was done at the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Department of National Defence. In fiscal year 1984-85, this program was cut to $6.6 million.
The current situation, as I understand it, is that there is only funding of approximately $1 million, with research primarily being carried out at the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. In an appearance before the Standing Committee on Research, Science and Technology last week, the President of the National Research Council, Dr. Larkin Kerwin, told us how difficult it would be to gear up for another program in the area of hydrogen research. I would like to quote a few words from his submission:
If we were to start up the Division again, it would take a very long time and a very great amount of money. I know that there is a government commission going around the country at the moment examining the problem of alternate energy sources, but if it were to start up again at NRC, it would take us a long time to reassemble this team.
So there we have the Conservative approach to research and development. They come into office, close down the energy division, then they set up, under the auspices of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, a commission to explore the potential for developing alternative energy sources. This is, of course, after they have cut all the research in the area of alternative energies. Then they start thinking about pursuing a national mission in the area of the development of hydrogen. If that is not an example of reverse logic or short-sighted thinking, I would personally have difficulty finding a better one.
I would like to say a word to the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville about the particular motion we are debating today. He is suggesting that a Canadian hydrogen authority be established. I think it may be implicit in his motion, but I would like to say to him that it is my belief, and perhaps understood in the report of the Advisory Group on Hydrogen Opportunities, that this authority will not actually do the research but will ensure that research is done. It will, of course, need to have appropriate funding to prime research in the private sector.
I also want to say to the Member that I understand him to be proposing this as a national mission for Canada, but I do not think he is suggesting that this is perhaps the only area in which we need to consider a major project. I personally believe that in order to increase our spending on research and development, and in order to ensure that our industry is
Supply
competitive in world markets in the next century, we are going to have to embark upon perhaps a number of major research projects. One could very well be in the area of hydrogen.
I think a space station has tremendous benefits for Canadian industry, if we can get a handle on the costs, and if the Government will be up front with us and let us know exactly what is happening in that particular area. Dr. Kerwin of the National Research Council mentioned a number of other areas where the National Research Council is considering what could be called major projects, such as in the area of health care technology, which would try to obtain reductions in costs in health care for Canadians. Again, I would ask the Member if this is really not his motivation in putting this motion forward. I think he is suggesting that certainly this is an area worthy of consideration as a major project, but I do not think he is saying it is the only area.
In conclusion, I want to agree with one of the comments the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville made when he was engaged in an exchange with the Minister of Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle). The Minister was talking about the need to get international partners involved in this type of major undertaking. No one can quarrel with the idea of getting partners in an undertaking of this nature. However, what 1 think the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville was saying is that there has to be a number of areas where Canadians can take leadership, where Canadians can show the world how to do it and where other countries, for once, will have to come to us to buy technology we have developed rather than vice versa.
What the Minister may have in mind by "collaboration", is the type of thing that has happened with the RadarSat project. We had a proposal to develop a radar satellite, which in many respects corresponds much more to Canadian needs and to the capacities of our industry than the space station project. We have cut off some of the features of the radar satellite so that under the present proposal being considered by the Government its capabilities would be much less than what was initially proposed. We then went to the Americans, the British and perhaps other countries and said: "We would like you to do major parts of this particular project", in order to reduce Canadian funding. Now, basically, we cannot proceed with the project unless we get the British, in particular, to proceed with their part of it. The situation we have now is that the decision to proceed with an important Canadian priority is not being made here in Ottawa but is being made by Mrs. Thatcher in London.
If that is the kind of international collaborative effort the Minister is proposing, I would say that Canadians want no part of that kind of major project. Canadians want a project into which we can put our wits and our abilities and where Canadians can, for once, develop some kind of technology, as in the area of our space communications, where we have developed a technology and capability which are recognized and renowned throughout the world.

Madam Speaker, I would first like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Laurier (M. Berger) and wish him a happy birthday.

In respect of some of the questions the Hon. Member has posed during the course of his speech, he wonders whether I had suggested that a national mission should mean that we do not continue to encourage the development of science and technology in other areas.
I do not want to have what I have suggested misunderstood. I think we have to look back on good examples of national missions of the past to get a measure of where, in the context of our over-all research and development thrust, this should be placed.
For example, let us consider the declaration of a national mission by President Kennedy to make the United States first in space. This meant the mobilization of abundant resources and the co-operation across a broad spectrum of American industry, academia and government laboratories in order to accomplish this mission, which was the dominant mission in the United States. This did not come at a cost to the rest of the research and development thrust in the United States. Indeed, at the same time there was a tremendous increase in resources being made available in the United States to all aspects of science, as well as to more research funding and to better quality teaching of science in universities and high schools.
A national mission is quite different from an area of emphasis. There is any number of areas on which we can have some emphasis. There are certainly possibilities for smaller, more narrowly defined missions. But none can take the measure of the type of national mission that is conceived of in this proposition. It challenges the imagination with respect to what it is capable of doing. It will generate new science, new industry and new engineering.
Let me point out that in developing export forms of hydrogen technology we can even look to photosynthesis, which is the biological process of primacy from which under natural conditions hydrogen really is the first product. We can talk about translating biology into engineering, to use sunlight directly to generate hydrogen. There is fantastic scope to this type of mission.
To compare this with the contribution of Canada to the space platform is to compare apples to oranges. There is no possible way that our involvement there can have the industrial and technological pay-off, diffusion of new technologies and the saleable products that this type of mission would generate.
I agree with the Hon. Member, we must continue in the broad scope of all the deficiencies that exist in Canada with respect to our standing internationally in science and research and development and we cannot let those other areas go. This
is the type of mission that is not completely predictable in what it will require. We must have an abundant storehouse of knowledge, skills and education in the sciences and engineering right across the board to make this mission work.
Industry needs to do its job in developing its technology. This is an area in which the involvement of Government in providing leadership is necessary. It is also necessary that Government make a contribution to the expenditures that will not yield an immediate pay-off to industry and which therefore will not draw the type of investment during the early years in many areas that will be necessary in the long term to develop.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-A CANADIAN HYDROGEN AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I participate in the debate today on the opposition motion introduced by my colleague and the critic for the New Democratic Party for science and technology. The motion is that, in essence, the Government undertake a hydrogen mission. I would like to discuss some of the concepts in the motion that we have in front of us today.
When I was critic for my Party for the science and technology portfolio after the 1984 election I was concerned at that time, and I still am, that Canada play a leading role in developing alternate technologies. At that time we were in the midst of the energy crisis. We were told that fossil fuels were fast running out. We saw the price of gasoline at the pumps jump almost on a daily basis. There was a tremendous economic shock not only to the pocket-books of the average Canadian but also to the many industries that used gasoline as their source of energy.
There was a great deal of concern at that time in terms of developing alternate energies. The Government of the day introduced home insulation type programs, programs which were meant to reduce the consumption of energy. Many of those programs were successful in reducing our dependence on fossil fuels, on energy.
It became necessary to look for other sources. We all recognize that fossil fuel is a non-renewable source of energy. Eventually, we will run out of this fuel. Thus the search goes on.
Parliament recognized that when in 1980-81 it struck a special committee of Members of Parliament on alternative energy and oil substitution. The committee produced quite an intriguing report. It was a very thorough study of Canada's energy needs at that particular time. It attempted to project the demand for energy as well as the supply for energy into the future. It attempted as well to look at some alternatives. The major conclusion that the committee drew was that Canada should move to develop a hydrogen based energy system.
I look now at another report entitled National Mission for Canada. As I look through the report I find that many of the matters that were stated in 1981 are repeated in the report of June, 1987. Again, it presented the conclusion that we must move to a hydrogen based economy, and that there is a role for
March 30, 1988

Government to play in moving the country toward that objective.
As other speakers have pointed out in today's debate, there are various reasons why we should move in that direction. The first is the fact that fossil fuels are non-renewable and therefore a finite source of energy. We have to look for other sources.
Hydrogen is a beautiful alternative. Its source is from an infinite form of energy, either from hydrogen dams, that is, energy generated by the movement of water, or from another interesting and exciting area involving solar energy.
I have been intrigued in this field for a long time. I went to California in 1980 to look at a project that was being developed in which solar cells were combined to produce electricity and then through an electrolysis system hydrogen was produced. The hope was that we would have energy from sunlight and from water, two of the most common items on our planet. Through this process all regions of the world could become self-sufficient with this form of energy, hydrogen.
Since that time there has been another important aspect that has been introduced in this debate. I believe it was around 1982-83 that the Environmental Protection Agency of the United States issued its report, followed soon thereafter by reports from other eminent scientific bodies that warned us that there was a clock ticking out the time. With the consumption of carbon fuels the earth and its atmosphere was being filled with carbon particles that would create a greenhouse effect which would have a devastating impact on the climate of the world.
When that report first came out I rose in my place and asked the then Minister of Energy if he was aware of this report and if he was prepared to give the same grants and subsidies to alternative energies that were clean, like hydrogen, that he was at that time giving to the nuclear industry and to the oil industry. At that time the Minister of Energy pooh-poohed my concern and stated that it had absolutely nothing to do with the burning of fossil fuels and the types of grants and subsidies given to the oil industry, and that he did not see the relevance of my question whatsoever.
It is true, and in fairness I must say that the then Minister of the Environment was concerned with the problems posed by the greenhouse effect. That Minister did give me some more honest answers. He indicated that the Government was aware of the greenhouse effect on Canada, that it was actively studying it, there was an awareness of it, and that something down the road would have to be done.
Since the report came out on the greenhouse effect, we see reports being made public by a committee of the Government that illustrates the greenhouse effect on Canada. Many of the low-lying coastal regions would be flooded. The area from which I come in southern Saskatchewan would become desert.
Supply
Certainly, other areas of Canada would benefit. The more northern regions would become more hospitable in terms of agriculture and a place in which to live, and there would be a shift of population to the more northern areas of Saskatchewan, Ontario, Manitoba and Alberta.
There is no doubt that a crisis is looming. We can begin to see some of the first effects of the greenhouse effect. We can see small increases in the mean temperature on the globe. Every scientist has predicted that if the trend continues there could be a warming of three, four or five degrees. This would have catastrophic effects on Canada.
In 1981 the committee made the following observation in terms of the greenhouse effect. The report stated that to most Canadians the difference of two, three, four, or five degrees is not very much. We live in a country where we can see temperatures change 10 or 20 degrees Celsius within a matter of hours or days, so what is so great about having the mean global temperature increase by a few degrees Celsius?
The report stated:
Thus it has been suggested that the melting of the polar ice caps could be triggered by a mean global temperature rise of only one to three degrees Celsius. In fact, from the peak of the last glacial period 20,000 to 16,000 years ago to the peak of the warm interglacial period we are presently living in, the mean temperature of the ocean rose only 2 degrees Celsius and the mean global temperature rose only 5 degrees Celsius.
We can see the effects of an increase in the global temperature of only a few degrees. The difference between the ice age and our present period is only the difference of a mean global temperature of some 5 degrees Celsius. How delicate is the planet and its atmosphere!
We have received warnings from scientists that the clock is ticking away, and it requires global action.
Fossil fuels are running out and at the same time a catastrophe is beginning to occur. Hydrogen is the solution to both of those problems. Hydrogen is the cleanest fuel that anyone could hope for. Its only by-product is water vapour. Common sense, and what the best scientific minds are telling us is that that is the direction in which we have to go, and there is not all that much time.
There might be 20 to 50 years in terms of the amount of fossil fuels we have, depending upon how good we are with our technology. If we can produce more efficient cars and more efficient home insulation we can stretch out the amount of fossil fuel that we have. But eventually we must recognize that it will run out. Why not begin to develop something that one's intelligence and common sense tells us we must begin to do.
I was encouraged to hear the Minister's remarks in his response to the motion introduced by the New Democratic Party. I think that the Minister understands that this is the direction in which we have to go. He agrees that Canada has a role to play. Both the House of Commons report and the report that came out in June, 1987 state that we are in a uniquely fine position to develop and to take the lead in developing

March 30, 1988
Supply
hydrogen technology. Yet there was nothing in the statements and comments of the Minister that would suggest to me that the Government is ready to take the lead. This is what is required. We need a Government that is ready to take the lead.
I am not suggesting that the new hydrogen technology be entirely developed by governments. My colleague did not suggest that. But it does require leadership. It does require an organization or some entity to pull together members from the academic community, members from industry, and various provincial utilities to start creating a working group, to start developing an agenda, to start putting some money into place, to start initiating definite research projects, and to begin to break down what has to be done to get us into the hydrogen society and start mapping out what the steps should be.
I am not suggesting some grand over-all plan because there has to be flexibility. As technology changes and new discoveries are made there must be flexibility in order to change the agenda. But there must be some entity to begin to pull it all together.
There was nothing in the statement of the Minister that would indicate to me that the Government is ready to take that step and start calling upon Canadians from labour, universities, and from the business community and challenge Canadians to a national mission. I would suggest that Canadians are ready to undertake such a mission. Canadians are concerned about their future, not only the future of the country but the future of the world. Canadians are concerned about acid rain, the greenhouse effect, and about what type of world our children will be living in.
I think Canadians would welcome a Government which would issue a challenge. I think they would welcome a Government which would come forward and say: "We believe that there is a way to save our environment, our forests, and our lakes, and that Canada has a major part to play". Canadians will respond to such a challenge. However, we need a Government with some vision, imagination, and will-power to take the lead.
I should like to refer to another aspect of the comments of my colleague. He expressed concern about whether a mission could indeed be undertaken in view of the agreement which the Government has signed with the Government of the United States.
Certainly my understanding of the agreement is that it severely restricts what Canadian society can do. It also restricts our ability for public and private co-operation in joint ventures. There is no doubt, if we are to develop into a hydrogen economy, that we will need some leadership by Government. There is no doubt that we will have to spend tax dollars, give some special tax considerations, and perhaps provide subsidies. The public role is essential to undertaking a project which might be a 10-year or a 20-year one. We need public participation.
I question whether the trade agreement between Canada and the United States, which the Government wants us to ratify at a later date, will allow for that type of co-operation. My reading of the agreement indicates that it locks us forever into a society and economy where the private sector will have to do it all. It seems to me that government participation is something that is restricted in the agreement because it would be considered unfair competition.
I wish the Minister would have addressed himself to the following question: Is it now impossible, with the free trade agreement, to undertake a national mission which also has some economic benefits? I suppose we could always take on a national mission, as did the Americans when they landed on the moon or created a space station, with minimal economic benefits. However, a project like the development of technologies that bring us into a hydrogen age is different. There are definite trade and economic implications. I fear that the agreement which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the President of the United States have signed severely restricts our ability to undertake such a joint mission.
In that vein let us look at the nations of the world which I feel are some of the most successful economic examples. In Japan and Germany co-operative systems are in place. There is co-operation among business, labour, and government. The trade agreement will put us into the type of economic development that I would call the Rambo economics which we find in the United States today where the public sector has been so totally and drastically reduced that it is very difficult to develop a co-operative approach among various elements in society whether they be labour, business, or government.
In conclusion, the motion calls for a new vision or the vision of a new age and a new technology sensitive to the environment. It calls for a technology which can be decentralized and used in localities and which destroys the monopolistic power of a few large utilities or corporations over the lives of millions of people.
As well it calls for a new concept of implementation, a concept of co-operation or working together to define a national goal or mission in which various elements in society come together and in a national way attempt to achieve the goal.
I am very grateful to have had the opportunity to address the motion introduced this afternoon by the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy). It is a good motion. I am pleased as well by the various contributions made this afternoon by Hon. Members of the other political Parties. Hopefully some day we will see such a co-operative approach being adopted by whatever Government is in power at the time. For the sake of the future of the country and the future of the globe, I hope the day will come soon.

Madam Speaker, I listened with considerable care to the remarks of the Hon. Member. I in no way dispute his sincerity, because I know him to be that sort of individual
March 30, 1988

and Member. However, I thought that we were hearing a paean to the new Jerusalem rather than a discourse on hydrogen.
I wonder whether the Hon. Member could answer two questions. The first one relates to the region from which he hails-western Canada. Would he be in agreement with the idea that any kind of national hydrogen mission or project should be truly national in scope and should have, at least in its first decades, two components-one based on hydrocarbons, with the immense surpluses of natural gas which exist in western Canada, and the second based on the obvious electrolysis involvement with a base in Manitoba through to Newfoundland and abundant hydroelectricity providing the opportunity to create hydrogen from our fresh water sources? Could the Hon. Member give us the guidance of his vast knowledge and experience in that regard?
Also, with reference to the Hon. Member's comment about there being minimal economic benefit from the Canadian space program, has he studied the testimony given before the Standing Committee on Research, Science and Technology in June of last year when Mr. Champagne gave his very strong statements on that subject?
If I may, I should like to quote briefly what Mr. Champagne said:
Canada's commitment to participate in the United States' space station program creates a unique opportunity for development and application of new technologies appropriate to Canada.
He went on to say:
The link between space and terrestrial activity is established through hydrogen, a ubiquitous element in the space environment for propulsion and life support, and in the industrial infrastructure for chemical process and energy applications.
Finally Mr. Champagne said:
There is at present a window of opportunity for Canada to exploit its natural advantages in order to establish a broader key role in space and the corresponding technological leadership in hydrogen technology and its application.
He went on to cite a number of examples of how it could be done.
Given the fact that upwards of 600 tonnes daily of hydrogen go to waste in the atmosphere in western Canada, which would be more than enough to fuel a major hydrogen research program today, and given the fact that the experts in our nation on space and hydrogen have shown the clear linkage between those opportunities, could the Hon. Member give us the benefit of his wisdom in commenting on those statements?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-A CANADIAN HYDROGEN AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I enjoyed the comments and questions raised by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Edwards). First, he is concerned about the regional differences and the regional implications for the development of hydrogen. Of course, east of Manitoba, hydrogen would be using the electricity from the hydro
Supply
projects of Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec and further east. In the West, of course, as the Hon. Member pointed out, there is a fair amount of natural gas. That could be used to create hydrogen through ammonia.
In fact, in the early 1980s when we were still in power in the Province of Saskatchewan, I approached my colleagues in the Government to support research which would use the ammonia many farmers already have on their farms and to do research into the conversion of that so that farmers in Saskatchewan could start driving their tractors on hydrogen. I believe that the technological innovations that would occur in western Canada in the first phase of developing a hydrogen economy could conceivably be different than those in eastern Canada, as one step in the process.
We from western Canada must as well face the fact that not only are fossil fuels running out but there is an environmental problem with fossil fuels. At this time, hydrogen helps western Canada, and particularly Saskatchewan, where there is heavy oil by allowing the utilization of heavy oil.
Eventually, we in western Canada must recognize that fossil fuels are running out, that an environmental time clock is ticking away. We in western Canada would want to see some of the development and technologies necessary to develop hydrogen located in western Canada as well. We would want part of that development pie. That is why I think it is important that we get on the bandwagon.
My colleague has pointed out that Alberta already has a lead in the development and utilization of hydrogen because of the oil industry which can produce the technologies. It is a natural lead, so let us build on that lead that we have in western Canada.
The Hon. Member's second point dealt with the space station. What I was trying to get at was the difference between investing the billion odd dollars involved in a space station and investing in a project like the development of hydrogen. Common sense tells us that there is quite a difference in the pay-back period and the application time. That is not to say that a space station would not have economic benefits and impacts, but I suggest that if it becomes a choice, and in this day and age it very often becomes a choice because of scarce resources, I would definitely choose investing in something like hydrogen over spending $1 billion on making a contribution to a space station over which we have no control. We would be junior partners in someone else's project. As well, doing something that could begin to be a solution to the problem of the greenhouse effect, doing something that would guarantee us sources of energy when the fossil fuels run out, is much more important than investing in a space station.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for his eloquent portrayal of the problems Canada and the world face with the greenhouse effect and with the rapid transition that we will experience.

March 30, 1988

I am sure the Hon. Member realizes that the world has been much warmer, geologically speaking. The University of Saskatchewan recently dug up some leaves, not fossil leaves, from Ellesmere Island which showed a climate very similar to the climate now in northern Oregon. Forty-five million years ago, there was that sort of climate at latitude 78 degrees which right now is a very desolate tundra, devoid of much flora and fauna.
I would like to ask the Hon. Member how he sees nuclear energy tying into the bigger picture. I ask that because the Hon. Member has dealt with the making of hydrogen, but if we make hydrogen from fossil fuels, we still have the problem of putting more carbon dioxide into the air, the problem of the greenhouse effect.
The standing committee is currently looking at Canada's nuclear role and will take a look at the experience in Sweden where they are in the process of phasing it out and at the experience in France where they are building it as rapidly as they can. I would be curious to know what the Hon. Member's feelings are on this subject.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-A CANADIAN HYDROGEN AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to thank my colleague from Calgary for the very legitimate question he has posed. Personally, I have always been very uncomfortable about the nuclear industry. On the one hand, when it is operating properly, it creates clean electricity, if we could only know what to do with the waste. On the other hand, we are also taking such a tremendous risk for such a tremendously long period of time with such a large part of the globe.
The accidents that occurred in Three Mile Island and in the Soviet Union will contaminate large areas of the globe for hundreds if not thousands of years to come. It is a gamble. How many more disasters can the earth afford? How many more Three Mile Islands and Chernobyl can we experience? We cannot continue taking those risks.
We must develop sources of electricity other than nuclear sources. As well, the cost effectiveness of the nuclear industry is something we must now look at seriously. Certainly there are many utilities in the United States that wish they had never come across the word "nuclear" because of the economic costs.
My hope is that we can get abundant energy from sunlight through solar cells, from hydro-electric power plants, from tides, from the temperature difference between different layers of the oceans. These are all possible infinite sources of energy.
I hope we can develop those, tie them in with hydrogen and indeed find something that is clean, safe and cost-effective.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-A CANADIAN HYDROGEN AUTHORITY
speechtext:
First, Madam
Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) for the very positive motion he has moved today. I take this opportunity to wish the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) a happy birthday, I also want the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville to know that several of our colleagues, including the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin), work very hard on that crucial issue of hydrogen technology.
As Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology, the Honourable Frank Oberle, I am proud to speak to you today about the government's accomplishments to date, the commitments we have made and our plans for the future in this vital field. The federal Government has made a firm commitment to give priority to science and technology and, over the past three years, it has been able to demonstrate its leadership in this field in a number of ways: by launching a major space program, increasing funding to the three granting councils, financing the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research, and forming the Advisory Committee on Hydrogen Opportunities, on which I would now like to say a few words.
The Advisory Committee on Hydrogen Opportunities was established by our government as an instrument to thoroughly analyze a technology with strong worldwide potential and to determine how Canada could develop new expertise. The Committee members are eminent specialists in the private and public sectors. One of the Committee's recommendations has been that Canada set itself the objective of being the first to cross the "hydrogen threshold", that is, to develop and call our own the best available technologies utilizing hydrogen for the production of liquid fuels and other chemical products.
As has been its practice for all major S&T initiatives, the Government is currently holding extensive consultations with those industries concerned with the development of hydrogen-related technologies.
You will no doubt recall that the federal microelectronics strategy, representing some 90 million, was drawn up in the same mannner, in direct co-operation with Canadian industry. Once the consultation process is over, the Government will make a sound decision on development initiatives for this sector. Clearly, though, we cannot put all our eggs in one basket. The National Conference on Technology and Innovation held in Toronto last January gave us an opportunity to assess our progress to date and identify future challenges.
I would now like to discuss the changes brought about by our government to ensure that science and technology assume their rightful role in strengthening the national economy. The agreement for the first national S&T policy was signed by the federal, provincial and territorial ministers on March 12, 1987. With this agreement, the various governments undertook to promote entrepreneurship and to recognize the importance of
March 30, 1988

R&D for Canada's economic, social, cultural and regional development.
The Government recently prepared a decision-making framework with which it can co-ordinate and direct the $4 billion spent each year on S&T. It was also in March 1987 that the Government launched the new national strategy designed to ensure that Canadian S&T efforts are effectively guided and targetted.
This strategy can be implemented only in a climate of cooperation between the governments and the public and private sectors. Innovaction covers specific programs totalling $100 million. On August 19, 1987, $11 million more were allocated for 1987-88 to the Matching Fund Policy, a program that has been so popular that all the funds have been committed. It is a $700 million co-operation program between the private and public sectors to which the Government has contributed so far $378 million.
To go back to Innovaction: On August 25, 1987, $30 million of new funds went to the Unsolicited Proposals Program and an amount of $7 million was also added for microelectronic research. And on August 27, 1987: $28 millions of new funds over four years for the Industrial Research Assistance Program; and on September 4, 1987: $12.3 over four years for the Technology Inflow Program. There is also the famous $3.5 million Canadian Manufacturing Advanced Technology Exchange program.
Under the Canada-Quebec Agreement, the 6.9 million dollars in S&T grants awarded by Ottawa and Quebec to small and medium-sized businesses have generated more than 28 million dollars in business investment. It was also under this 100-million-dollar agreement that the National Optical Institute was established in Sainte-Foy.
The membership of the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology, chaired by Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), includes noted scientists, teachers, and industry and labour representatives who provide the Government with pertinent analyses and enlightened opinions about federal S&T policies. The National Advisory Board, the Standing Com-mitee on Research, Science and Technology and the Council of Science and Technology Ministers all represent organizational measures designed to support and promote S&T initiatives, make us more competitive internationally, and sustain economic growth in Canada.
It is obvious today that tomorrow's jobs and our future prosperity depend on our scientific and technological capital. The technological challenge that faces Canadians today does not come only from inside our borders. We live in a "global village," as Marshall McLuhan said, and all countries will henceforth be interdependent in more ways than one. Science and technology have become the driving force of the new international economic order, and Canada has also entered the race for technological survival.
Supply
When we speak of scientific potential, Canada's reputation is already established, and Canadian high technology is already known outside our borders. With free trade, Canada will become a full partner with its neighbour to the south, and not only from the economic standpoint, but also, and above all, from the standpoint of innovation.
The foundations have been laid for the scientific and technological revival that the government promised at the beginning of its mandate.
At the National Conference in Toronto, the Prime Minister announced an additional $1.3 billion for S&T, including $240 million for the establishment of networks of centres of excellence, and 80 million for scholarships in science and engineering.
This week, after the Regional Conference in Vancouver, the Hon. Minister of State for Science and Technology explained just how these scholarships would be awarded.
The networks of centres of excellence will be operational by the end of 1988. They will involve researchers and scientists based in small and large universities throughout the country who will conduct world-class research in areas important to Canada's long-term competitiveness.
The networks of centres of excellence will also help to strengthen links and intensify exchanges between university researchers, industry and government, which is imperative if we want to meet the technological challenge on all fronts.
The networks of centres of excellence will use the latest telecommunication systems, a field in which Canada has a worldwide reputation.
As for university research funded by the three granting councils, a budget of $3.4 billion is being allocated to these bodies over five years.
On the basis of the consensus reached at the national conference and the recommendations made by the participants, we have instituted a series of five regional conferences, the first of which took place in Vancouver at the beginning of the week. The other regional conferences will be held in Regina, Hamilton, Montreal and Saint-John, New Brunswick.
These conferences are pursuing the impetus of the national conference to enable more Canadians from all parts of the country to contribute to the new national S&T perspective and add a regional dimension.
We expect the science and engineering scholarships to offer further encouragement to students to pursue careers in the natural sciences and engineering.
As the Minister of State for Science and Technology announced in Vancouver this week, at least half of the 2,500

March 30, 1988
Supply
scholarships will go to women in order to produce a higher number of women scientists and engineers.
We will thus ensure that our industries will in the future never lack the highly qualified personnel to keep Canada in the forefront of international competition.
Another government initiative is likely to have a marked impact on Canada's future prosperity, because it is aimed at every citizen of the country.
At the Toronto conference, the Minister of State for Science and Technology announced the launching of a $ 10-million national campaign to alert the public to the importance of S&T to our country's future.
The national public awareness campaign is an important component of Innovaction. This is a long-term campaign involving governments, industry, educators, scientists and nonscientists, creators and users.
It is of vital importance to develop the scientific side of our culture by stimulating the intellectual genius of our citizens and nurturing their curiosity.
As part of this awareness campaign, an enhanced program, which we have redubbed Science Culture Canada, will provide increased assistance to non-governmental organizations initiating various projects and activities aimed at furthering public understanding of the role and impact of S&T.
A new component of Science Culture Canada is aimed directly at young Canadians, our citizens of tomorrow.
We all realize how important it is to inculcate in our young people, and particularly in our young women, a vision for their own future and a desire to contribute to the progress of their country.
At the same time, Canadians will become aware of the growing interaction between science and technology and the country's economic growth. They will no longer see innovation as a threat to their job security, but rather as a challenge designed to improve the quality of life.
Lastly, I will speak to you about the creation of the Department of Industry, Science and Technology, DIST, a new organization that clearly reflects the Government's determination to give precedence to the integration of high technology in order to stimulate the competitive ability of our industry.
DIST will develop a national industrial policy which will stress advanced technologies, as much to assist in reorganizing traditional industries as to encourage activity in strategic new sectors.
Only a concerted effort on the part of the industrial and scientific communities can ensure the integration of technological knowledge in Canadian industry, and one of the main objectives of DIST will be to mobilize potential for action and production and to catalyze efforts.
Our common goal is to improve Canada's ability to compete on an international scale, not only by offering the best we have, but also by diversifying our goods and services.
We assure you that we are fully aware of the fact that the development of new technologies depends, above all, on basic research and on those who devote themselves to it.
During the past two years, the Government explicitly committed itself to improving basic research in Canada through the action of three Granting Councils, and DIST will adopt the same approach.
In conclusion, henceforward, science and technology will no longer be confined to a mere support role for society, because they have become the driving force of our social and economic growth.
In 1986-87, the Government invested $4.2 billion in science and technology, of which $2.6 billion were pumped into research and development. This makes the government the most important source of funding for all the R&D done in Canada.
The initial effects of the national conference already allow us to anticipate that the university, scientific and industrial communities will be equally willing to accept the challenge the Prime Minister gave them when he said: "The government is being challenged to do more, and we willingly accept this challenge! In return, I am asking what you intend to do to establish the new industrial, technological and educational structures that Canada needs to become a leader on the markets of the world."
Thank you for your attention, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I listened carefully to the Hon. Member's speech. I also read the comments she made last June when she asked Mr. Richard Champagne, and I quote: "If we were called upon to supply hydrogen to the American Space Program, where would our facilities be located and how would the hydrogen be brought to the American astrosupport centres?" Mr. Champagne answered, and I quote: "In the short term we clearly have very important reserves of hydrogen in the west. We have just taken stock in Alberta and we have determined that over 600 tonnes a day are being burnt or left to escape."
I would like to ask the Hon. Member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Duplessis):

Given the abundance of hydrogen in the West and understanding that the long-term future of hydrogen development and strategy would be based in hydro-electricity or nuclear energy, is it possible, in the Hon. Member's view, that the initial research and development might be done in the West and may then gradually spread, given the economics of the technology, through to central and eastern Canada? I would appreciate the Hon. Member's comments on that.
March 30, 1988

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Science and Technology)
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-A CANADIAN HYDROGEN AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for his question. As Parliamentary Secretary, I can inform the Hon. Member that I have no objection to research being done in Western Canada, and more specifically in Alberta, since the Hon. Member is from that Province. I know for a fact that research is also being done in the province of Quebec.
However, in his recommendations Mr. Champagne mentioned the provinces that had the potential for becoming major hydrogen suppliers. He mentioned British Columbia, Manitoba, Quebec and Newfoundland. He added that Ontario could also become a hydrogen-producing province.
Madam Speaker, I think the development and production of hydrogen technology is a discipline of the future, and I believe that both research and production might increase Canada's prosperity, in the near future and perhaps also in the long term.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-A CANADIAN HYDROGEN AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we have been listening to government Members speak on the question of hydrogen and its importance. I do not think I have heard any greater hypocrisy than that. I say this seriously because of the situation that has existed in the last three and a half years.
When the Government came to power in 1984, there was a plan to spend between $8 million and $9 million a year on hydrogen and electrical chemical research. The spending plan for hydrogen and electrical chemical research this year is $1 million, through the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources.
The Government completely disbanded the research and development projects on hydrogen that were undertaken by the National Research Council. If the Government is so concerned about hydrogen research, why did it take that action? Why have we lost a whole generation of science and research in this country?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Science and Technology)
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-A CANADIAN HYDROGEN AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am surprised to hear my Opposition colleague say we are hypocrites. The Hon. Member knows perfectly well that under the Canada-Quebec Agreement, we contributed towards the facilities at the electrochemical centre in Shawinigan, which is also active in this area.
Madam Speaker, I think, I hope and I am prepared to assume that the Hon. Member spoke hastily, and I trust he will take back what he said.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-A CANADIAN HYDROGEN AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my comments were not directed at the Member who just spoke, but were certainly directed at the
Supply
Government. I certainly do not intend to retract the comments 1 made because they were directed at the Government. I think that was quite clear.
The fact remains that the Government has destroyed a whole generation of research on hydrogen as a result of its budget- cutting, beginning in November, 1984. Clearly, the Government has destroyed the hydrogen research that was undertaken.
On March 3, 1988, when opening a liquid hydrogen plant in Quebec, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) said:
Hydrogen has the potential over the next 20 years to play a role in upgrading fossil fuels, such as Western Canada's heavy oil. During this time, if we can develop commercially feasible technologies, hydrogen could augment the existing wide range of energy sources available to Canada.
The Government's own news release states:
Mr. Masse said the Government of Canada plans to develop a long term action plan for hydrogen use following a report from the Federal Advisory Group on Hydrogen Opportunities released on August 26, 1987. The report identified several potential uses for hydrogen and recommended a national hydrogen mission.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is supposed to know about energy in this country and the tremendous potential of hydrogen.
Let us compare what the Minister and the Hon. Member who just spoke said about the Government's record with what Mr. Larkin Kerwin, head of the NRC, said to the standing committee. After being questioned by the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy), Mr. Kerwin stated:
Concerning the hydrogen program, NRC's Energy Division has been closed down, as you know, and all of our alternate energy projects, except those very few that are connected with other divisions, have been closed down.
If we were to start up the Division again, it would take a very long time and a very great amount of money. I know that there is a government commission going around the country at the moment examining the problem of alternate energy sources but if it were to start up again at NRC, it would take us a long time to reassemble this team.
That is incredible when we consider this tremendous energy potential. Hydrogen makes up 75 per cent of the mass of the earth. It can enrich the tar sands in Alberta to enable us to obtain gasoline. Hydrogen can be made with water and methane, as well as through electrolysis.
It is projected that by the middle of the twenty-first century one-third of all our energy will be from electricity, one-third from hydrocarbons, and one-third from hydrogen. Yet what is the Government's record? It has been completely negative, destroying whatever research was going on in this country. It is incredible to hear the Government state what it will do with hydrogen when it has destroyed the programs that already existed.
It is significant to note that Canada can be at the forefront of hydrogen technology, if we have the will to do so. There are five requirements to develop an expertise in hydrogen. First, we need natural gas, which is currently the best source of

Supply
hydrogen. Second, we have abundant reserves of hydrogen-deficient hydrocarbons, such as heavy oil, which need upgrading and can be added to hydrogen to become a very valuable resource.
Third, we need a domestic electrolysis industry, with the ability to generate electricity from non fossil fuels.
The fifth requirement is the will to develop state-of-the-art hydrogen technology. I am sure that is possible once Canadians realize the importance of this element and the potential it has for replacing our diminishing non renewable resources.
Furthermore, the only byproduct of burning hydrogen is water vapour. Therefore, there is no environmental problem.
We only need the technology and the will of Government to develop this very powerful source of energy. It is unacceptable for the Government to continue to treat this simply as a topic of science and technology about which people want to hear. The Government must spend money.
This is not a new project. The Government has cut funding from $9 million in 1984 to $1 million this year, yet expects to develop a technology.
The Committee on Alternative Energy, chaired by Tom Lefebvre, suggested that the Government should spend $1 billion on hydrogen research over a five-year period. If the Government wants to take this seriously, it should begin doing something positive rather than stripping away the programs we already have.
